books.title: Exploration: Textbook of Science for Grade 9
books.edition: First Edition, April 2026 (Chaitra 1948) — new NCERT book for the 2026-27 session

source.method: chapter titles from the book's Contents page; topics from each chapter PDF's section headings

chapters.title: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science

topics.title: Models: Simplifying the Real World
objectives: Student can explain why science uses simplified models that keep only what matters for a given question
Student can decide which details to keep and which to ignore when modelling an everyday situation such as a cricket shot or a bicycle ride home
Student can explain why ignoring some details (like air resistance) is a deliberate choice, not a mistake
visualIdeas: a cricket ball hit for a six, with labels for the details kept (mass, speed, direction) and the details ignored (bat brand, ball colour)

topics.title: The Language of Science: Terms, Symbols, Units and Mathematics
objectives: Student can explain why everyday words like force, work and cell have precise meanings in science
Student can explain why standard (SI) units matter, using the aircraft fuel mix-up between pounds and kilograms
Student can describe an equation as a compact statement of how quantities are related, not just a calculation tool
visualIdeas: a pan balance with a 1 kg weight beside a table of quantities, symbols and units (m, v, F, I)

topics.title: Laws, Theories, Principles and Predictions
objectives: Student can distinguish a law (a regular pattern), a theory (an evidence-based explanation) and a principle (a broad guiding idea)
Student can explain that a scientific theory is not a guess and can change when new evidence appears
Student can turn an everyday prediction (such as rain from dark clouds) into questions that ask for measurable evidence
visualIdeas: a three-column card: law, theory, principle with one example each

topics.title: Estimation and Connected Branches of Science
objectives: Student can make a rough estimate (such as litres of air breathed in a day) and check whether it is reasonable
Student can explain why careful reasoning and approximate estimates are valued in science
Student can show how ideas from physics, chemistry, biology, earth science and mathematics connect in one real problem, such as how a mask works
visualIdeas: a web diagram linking a face mask to physics, chemistry, biology and mathematics

chapters.title: Cell: The Building Block of Life

topics.title: How to Study Cells?
objectives: Student can define resolution and magnification and explain why a microscope is needed to see cells
Student can compare what light microscopes and electron microscopes can resolve, using a size scale from eggs to cell parts
visualIdeas: a size ladder from 1 mm (fish egg) down to 1 µm with markers for the limits of the eye, light microscope and electron microscope

topics.title: Cell Membrane — The Universal Feature of a Cell
objectives: Student can describe the cell membrane as a selectively permeable boundary made largely of lipids
Student can explain diffusion and osmosis across the cell membrane
Student can predict what happens to a cell placed in isotonic, hypotonic and hypertonic solutions
visualIdeas: three cells side by side in isotonic, hypotonic and hypertonic solutions with arrows showing water movement

topics.title: Cell Wall — The Outer Covering of Cells
objectives: Student can explain why plant cells need a rigid cell wall made mainly of cellulose
Student can state that the cell wall is permeable while the membrane inside it is selectively permeable
visualIdeas: a plant cell with the cell wall and cell membrane drawn as two separate labelled layers

topics.title: The Cell Interior — A Coordinated Working System
objectives: Student can name the three basic parts of a cell: plasma membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus
Student can distinguish prokaryotic cells (nucleoid, no membrane-bound organelles) from eukaryotic cells
visualIdeas: side-by-side diagrams of a bacterial (prokaryotic) cell and an animal (eukaryotic) cell

topics.title: Organelles: Nucleus, Ribosomes, ER, Golgi Apparatus and Lysosomes
objectives: Student can explain why eukaryotic cells have organelles that carry out different life processes at the same time
Student can describe the nucleus as holding DNA in chromosomes and ribosomes as protein factories
Student can describe the roles of the endoplasmic reticulum (manufacturing), Golgi apparatus (packaging and shipping) and lysosomes (clean-up)
visualIdeas: a cell drawn as a factory with labelled departments: nucleus office, ribosome workbenches, ER production line, Golgi shipping, lysosome clean-up

topics.title: Organelles: Mitochondria, Plastids and Vacuoles
objectives: Student can describe mitochondria as the powerhouse of the cell
Student can describe plastids such as chloroplasts as centres for food synthesis in plant cells
Student can explain the role of vacuoles in storage and support, especially in plant cells
visualIdeas: a plant cell highlighting mitochondria, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole

topics.title: How do Normal Cells Grow and Divide?
objectives: Student can explain that organisms grow mainly because cells divide, not only because cells get bigger
Student can describe how an onion root tip is used to observe dividing cells
visualIdeas: an onion bulb with growing roots and a zoomed-in root tip showing cells at different stages

topics.title: Cell Division: Mitosis and Meiosis
objectives: Student can define cell division as the formation of new cells from pre-existing cells
Student can state that mitosis supports growth, repair and asexual reproduction
Student can state that meiosis is needed for sexual reproduction and creates genetic diversity
visualIdeas: a two-branch flowchart: one parent cell to two identical cells (mitosis) and to four different cells (meiosis)

topics.title: Cell Theory — The Unifying Principle of Biology
objectives: Student can state the cell theory and name the contributions of Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow
Student can explain that every cell has a definite life span and that cells which do not die when they should can lead to problems such as cancer
visualIdeas: a timeline 1838–1855 with Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow and their statements

topics.title: Why are Plant and Animal Tissues Different?
objectives: Student can explain how being fixed in one place versus moving about leads to different tissues in plants and animals
Student can relate the rigid cell wall of plant cells to support and the flexible animal cell to movement
visualIdeas: a tree and a running deer with their key tissue needs listed beside each

topics.title: Apical Meristem — How Do Plants Grow in Length?
objectives: Student can describe meristematic tissue as dividing tissue responsible for plant growth
Student can explain, using the onion root experiment, that growth in length happens at the tips of roots and shoots
visualIdeas: an onion bulb in a jar with roots measured on day 1, 2 and 3, and the root tip highlighted

topics.title: Lateral Meristem — How Do Plants Grow in Girth?
objectives: Student can explain that lateral meristem increases the girth of dicot stems
Student can relate annual rings in a cut tree trunk to yearly growth in girth
visualIdeas: a cut tree trunk showing annual rings with a counter for the age of the tree

topics.title: Intercalary Meristem — How Do Plants Grow After Being Cut?
objectives: Student can locate intercalary meristem at the base of internodes or just above nodes
Student can explain how grass grows again after being grazed or cut
visualIdeas: a grass stem with nodes and internodes labelled and regrowth arrows after cutting

topics.title: Permanent Tissues — Simple Tissues
objectives: Student can explain that permanent tissues form when cells stop dividing and become specialised
Student can compare parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma by structure and function
Student can describe the epidermis and stomata as protective and exchange structures of the plant
visualIdeas: a transverse section of a sunflower stem with parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma labelled

topics.title: Permanent Tissues — Complex Tissues: Xylem and Phloem
objectives: Student can describe xylem as the tissue that carries water and minerals
Student can describe phloem as the tissue that carries food made in the leaves
visualIdeas: a plant outline with blue arrows up the xylem and orange arrows through the phloem

topics.title: Epithelial Tissues — Structure and Functions
objectives: Student can describe epithelial tissue as closely packed cells covering the body and lining internal organs
Student can explain how the structure of epithelium protects against germs and controls exchange
visualIdeas: skin and the lining of the intestine shown as layers of tightly packed cells

topics.title: How Are Various Parts Connected in Our Body? (Connective Tissues)
objectives: Student can name blood, bone, cartilage, tendons and ligaments as connective tissues
Student can explain how each connects, supports or transports in the body
visualIdeas: a knee joint with bone, cartilage, tendon and ligament labelled, and a drop of blood beside it

topics.title: Can We Control Movement in Our Body? (Muscular Tissue)
objectives: Student can distinguish voluntary movements (skeletal muscle) from involuntary movements (smooth and cardiac muscle)
Student can describe skeletal muscle fibres as long, unbranched, multinucleate and striated
visualIdeas: three muscle cell types drawn side by side: skeletal, smooth and cardiac

topics.title: How Does the Body Sense, Communicate and Respond? (Nervous Tissue)
objectives: Student can describe nervous tissue as the body’s control and coordination network with the brain as control centre
Student can label the parts of a neuron such as dendrites, axon and axon terminals
visualIdeas: a labelled neuron with a signal travelling from dendrites to axon terminals

topics.title: The Musculoskeletal System
objectives: Student can name the parts of the musculoskeletal system: bones, muscles, joints, cartilage, tendons and ligaments
Student can explain that muscles pull on bones through tendons to produce movement under the control of the nervous system
visualIdeas: an arm with the biceps, tendon and bones labelled, contracting to lift the forearm

topics.title: Types of Joints
objectives: Student can describe ball and socket, hinge, pivot and fixed joints with an example of each
Student can relate the type of joint to the movement it allows, such as the shoulder versus the elbow
visualIdeas: four mini-diagrams: shoulder (ball and socket), elbow (hinge), neck (pivot), skull (fixed)

topics.title: Skeletal System
objectives: Student can describe the skeleton as a framework that supports the body and protects organs
Student can describe the skull, vertebral column with cartilage discs, and the rib cage and what each protects
Student can relate good posture to the health of the spine
visualIdeas: a front view of the human skeleton with the skull, spine and rib cage highlighted

topics.title: Describing Position
objectives: Student can describe the position of an object using a reference point (origin), distance and direction
Student can use positive and negative signs to show positions on either side of the origin along a straight line
visualIdeas: a number line road with the school as origin and houses at +200 m and −150 m

topics.title: Distance Travelled and Displacement
objectives: Student can distinguish distance travelled (a scalar) from displacement (a vector)
Student can calculate distance and displacement for an object that moves forward and back along a straight line
visualIdeas: an athlete’s path from start to a turning point and back, with distance and displacement arrows

topics.title: Average Speed and Average Velocity
objectives: Student can calculate average speed as total distance divided by total time
Student can calculate average velocity as displacement divided by time and explain when it differs from average speed
Student can relate a speedometer reading to instantaneous speed
visualIdeas: a speedometer next to a trip with distance, displacement and time labelled

topics.title: Average Acceleration
objectives: Student can define average acceleration as the change in velocity divided by the time taken
Student can state that acceleration is along the velocity when speed increases and opposite to it when speed decreases
visualIdeas: a bus speeding up and then braking, with velocity and acceleration arrows

topics.title: Plotting Graphs of Motion
objectives: Student can choose axes and scales to plot motion data from a table
Student can read values from a plotted graph
visualIdeas: a data table turning into points on a graph with labelled axes

topics.title: Position-Time Graphs
objectives: Student can draw position-time graphs for objects at rest and in uniform motion
Student can find velocity from the slope of a position-time graph
visualIdeas: a position-time graph with a straight line and a slope triangle

topics.title: Velocity-Time Graphs
objectives: Student can draw velocity-time graphs for increasing and decreasing velocity
Student can find acceleration from the slope of a velocity-time graph and displacement from the area under it
visualIdeas: a velocity-time graph with the slope and the shaded area under the line labelled

topics.title: Kinematic Equations for Motion in a Straight Line with Constant Acceleration
objectives: Student can derive v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as
Student can use the equations to solve problems such as the stopping distance of a braking vehicle
visualIdeas: three equation cards linked to a velocity-time graph
a car braking with its reaction distance and braking distance marked

topics.title: Motion in a Plane: Uniform Circular Motion
objectives: Student can define uniform circular motion as motion along a circle at constant speed
Student can explain that the direction of velocity changes continuously, so uniform circular motion is accelerated
Student can calculate the speed of an object in a circle from its radius and time period
visualIdeas: a ball on a circular path with velocity arrows drawn tangent at several points

topics.title: How Can We Classify Mixtures?
objectives: Student can classify mixtures as homogeneous or heterogeneous with everyday examples
Student can explain the difference between a mixture and a pure substance
visualIdeas: two beakers: salt water (uniform) and sand in water (visible particles)

topics.title: Solutions and Concentration
objectives: Student can identify the solute and solvent in a solution
Student can express concentration as mass by mass, mass by volume and volume by volume percentage
Student can calculate the concentration of a solution from given amounts
visualIdeas: a beaker of sugar solution with solute and solvent labelled and a percentage calculation beside it

topics.title: Solubility of Substances
objectives: Student can define solubility and a saturated solution
Student can describe how temperature affects the solubility of a substance
visualIdeas: a solubility versus temperature curve for a salt

topics.title: Crystallization
objectives: Student can describe crystallization as a method to obtain a pure solid from its solution
Student can explain why crystallization gives purer products than simple evaporation
visualIdeas: a hot saturated solution cooling to form crystals in a dish

topics.title: Distillation
objectives: Student can describe distillation for separating a solvent from a solution, and label the condenser and its role
Student can explain when fractional distillation is used to separate miscible liquids with close boiling points
visualIdeas: a labelled distillation apparatus with a flask, thermometer, condenser and receiver

topics.title: Paper Chromatography
objectives: Student can describe paper chromatography as a way to separate the components of a coloured mixture such as ink
Student can explain why different components travel different distances up the paper
visualIdeas: a strip of filter paper in a jar showing ink separated into bands of colour

topics.title: Separation of Two Immiscible Liquids
objectives: Student can identify immiscible liquids that form separate layers, such as mustard oil and water
Student can explain how a separating funnel separates two immiscible liquids by letting the lower layer run out through the stopcock
visualIdeas: a separating funnel with an oil layer above a water layer and the stopcock open

topics.title: Sublimation
objectives: Student can define sublimation and name substances that sublime
Student can describe how sublimation separates a sublimable solid from a mixture
visualIdeas: a china dish with a mixture heated under an inverted funnel, vapours solidifying on the funnel

topics.title: Suspensions
objectives: Student can describe the properties of a suspension: particles that are visible, settle on standing and can be filtered
Student can explain how centrifugation separates the components of a suspension
visualIdeas: a centrifuge tube before and after spinning, with solids packed at the bottom

topics.title: Colloids
objectives: Student can describe colloids as heterogeneous mixtures whose particles do not settle and pass through filter paper
Student can identify the dispersed phase and dispersion medium in common colloids such as emulsions
visualIdeas: three jars compared: solution, colloid and suspension with particle sizes marked

topics.title: Tyndall Effect
objectives: Student can describe the Tyndall effect as the scattering of a light beam by colloid particles
Student can use the Tyndall effect to tell a colloid from a true solution
visualIdeas: a torch beam passing through milky water (visible path) and salt water (no visible path)

topics.title: The Concept of Force and Measuring It
objectives: Student can recall that a force can start or stop motion, change speed or direction, and change shape
Student can measure the magnitude of a force with a spring balance and state its unit, the newton
visualIdeas: a spring balance pulling a block with the force reading in newtons

topics.title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces
objectives: Student can find the net force when several forces act on an object
Student can explain that balanced forces do not change motion while an unbalanced (net) force does
visualIdeas: a tug of war with equal and unequal teams and net-force arrows

topics.title: The Force of Friction: Often Overlooked but Always Present
objectives: Student can explain why an object does not move until the applied force exceeds friction
Student can explain why a moving object slows down and stops when the applied force is removed
Student can compare the force of friction on different surfaces using a spring balance
visualIdeas: a stack of coins sliding on wood, laminate and marble with different stopping distances

topics.title: Newton's First Law of Motion
objectives: Student can state Newton's first law of motion
Student can explain that zero net force means no change in velocity, including constant non-zero velocity
Student can describe inertia and how Galileo’s thought experiment on a frictionless surface led to the idea
visualIdeas: a block sliding forever on an imagined frictionless floor
position-time and velocity-time graphs for an object with no net force

topics.title: Newton's Second Law of Motion
objectives: Student can state Newton's second law as F = ma and define one newton
Student can describe how cart activities show that acceleration grows with net force and falls with mass
Student can use F = mg with g = 9.8 m s⁻² and explain why a fielder pulls the hands back while catching a fast ball
visualIdeas: a cart pulled with two different forces and its acceleration compared
a fielder pulling hands back while catching a cricket ball

topics.title: Newton's Third Law of Motion
objectives: Student can state Newton's third law: forces act in equal and opposite pairs on two different objects
Student can identify action-reaction pairs in examples such as pushing a table from a wheeled chair, recoil of a gun and a rocket
visualIdeas: a girl on a wheeled chair pushing a table, with paired force arrows on each object
a rocket with exhaust gases pushed down and the rocket pushed up

topics.title: Forces Acting on a System of Objects
objectives: Student can apply Newton's laws to two objects connected by a string
Student can find the acceleration of the system and the tension in the string
visualIdeas: two boxes joined by a string on a smooth surface with forces F and T marked

topics.title: Work Done by a Constant Force
objectives: Student can define work done by a constant force as force multiplied by displacement in the direction of the force
Student can state the unit of work, the joule
visualIdeas: a box pushed across a floor with force and displacement arrows

topics.title: When is Work Done Zero, Positive or Negative?
objectives: Student can identify situations where work done is zero even though a force acts
Student can distinguish positive work (force along displacement) from negative work (force opposite to displacement)
visualIdeas: three panels: holding a bag still (zero), lifting it (positive), friction on a sliding block (negative)

topics.title: The Work-Energy Theorem
objectives: Student can state that the net work done on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy
Student can use the work-energy theorem in simple numerical problems
visualIdeas: a ball being pushed and speeding up, with work equal to the gain in kinetic energy

topics.title: Forms of Energy
objectives: Student can list different forms of energy around us
Student can give examples of energy changing from one form to another
visualIdeas: an icon grid of energy forms: mechanical, heat, light, sound, chemical, electrical

topics.title: Kinetic Energy
objectives: Student can derive the expression for kinetic energy, ½mv²
Student can calculate the kinetic energy of a moving object
visualIdeas: two balls of different speed and mass with their kinetic energies compared

topics.title: Potential Energy
objectives: Student can explain potential energy as energy stored because of position or shape
Student can calculate gravitational potential energy as mgh
visualIdeas: a book on a shelf at height h above the floor with mgh marked

topics.title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
objectives: Student can state that mechanical energy is conserved when only gravity does work
Student can track kinetic and potential energy for a falling or swinging object
visualIdeas: a falling ball with bars for kinetic and potential energy at several heights

topics.title: Power
objectives: Student can define power as the rate of doing work and state its unit, the watt
Student can calculate power from work done and time taken
visualIdeas: two people climbing the same stairs in different times

topics.title: Simple Machines: Pulley and Inclined Plane
objectives: Student can define the mechanical advantage of a simple machine as load divided by effort
Student can explain how a pulley and an inclined plane make raising a load easier
visualIdeas: a pulley lifting a bucket from a well
a ramp used to push a barrel onto a truck

topics.title: Simple Machines: Lever
objectives: Student can identify the fulcrum, effort and load in a lever
Student can classify levers by the positions of fulcrum, effort and load and give an everyday example of each
visualIdeas: a seesaw lever with fulcrum, effort arm and load arm labelled

topics.title: Rediscovering the Roots of Atomic Theory
objectives: Student can describe the early ideas of indivisible particles from Acharya Kanada (parmanu) in India and Leucippus and Democritus (atomos) in Greece
Student can explain how Dalton’s atomic theory turned the idea of atoms into a scientific theory
visualIdeas: a timeline from Kanada and Democritus to Dalton (1808) with one idea under each name

topics.title: A Short Historical Journey Through Atomic Models: Thomson’s Model
objectives: Student can describe how experiments with cathode rays led to the discovery of the electron
Student can describe Thomson’s model of the atom and what it got right and wrong
visualIdeas: a cathode ray tube with the beam bending near a magnet
Thomson’s model drawn as a positive sphere with embedded electrons

topics.title: Testing Thomson’s Model: The Gold Foil Experiment
objectives: Student can describe Rutherford’s alpha particle scattering experiment and its observations
Student can explain how the observations led to a small, dense, positively charged nucleus
Student can state a limitation of Rutherford’s model
visualIdeas: alpha particles fired at gold foil: most pass through, a few deflect, very few bounce back

topics.title: Bohr’s Model of the Atom
objectives: Student can describe Bohr’s model with electrons in fixed orbits or shells (energy levels)
Student can explain how Bohr’s model addressed the problem with Rutherford’s model
visualIdeas: a nucleus with concentric shells labelled K, L, M and electrons on them

topics.title: What Components Contribute to the Mass of an Atom? Discovery of the Neutron
objectives: Student can explain why the mass of an atom is mostly in its nucleus
Student can describe Chadwick’s discovery of the neutron and compare the charge and mass of protons, neutrons and electrons
visualIdeas: a table comparing proton, neutron and electron by charge, mass and location

topics.title: Symbols of Elements
objectives: Student can describe how symbols for elements developed from Dalton’s pictures to Berzelius’s letters
Student can write the IUPAC symbols of common elements, including those from Latin names
visualIdeas: Dalton’s circle symbols beside modern letter symbols for the same elements

topics.title: Atomic Number and Mass Number
objectives: Student can define atomic number as the number of protons and mass number as protons plus neutrons
Student can find the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons from the atomic number and mass number
visualIdeas: an element box showing the symbol with mass number above and atomic number below

topics.title: How Are Electrons Distributed in Different Energy Levels?
objectives: Student can state the rule that a shell holds at most 2n² electrons and that shells fill in order
Student can write the electronic configuration of elements with small atomic numbers, such as sodium (2, 8, 1) and chlorine (2, 8, 7)
visualIdeas: shell diagrams for sodium and chlorine with electrons placed 2, 8, 1 and 2, 8, 7

topics.title: Combining Capacity of an Atom: Valency
objectives: Student can explain the octet rule and why atoms lose, gain or share electrons
Student can work out the valency of an element from its electronic configuration
visualIdeas: a sodium atom giving one electron and a chlorine atom completing its octet

topics.title: A Deeper Look into Atomic Structure: Isotopes and Isobars
objectives: Student can define isotopes and isobars with examples
Student can calculate the average atomic mass of an element from the abundance of its isotopes
Student can give uses of isotopes such as cobalt and iodine in medicine and uranium as a fuel
visualIdeas: three hydrogen isotopes side by side with their protons and neutrons
two isobars with the same mass number and different atomic numbers

topics.title: Law of Conservation of Mass
objectives: Student can show that mass is conserved in physical changes such as dissolving salt in water
Student can describe the vinegar and baking soda experiment in a closed set-up that shows mass is conserved in a chemical change
Student can state the law of conservation of mass and Lavoisier’s role in it
visualIdeas: a flask on a balance with a balloon of baking soda over vinegar, reading the same before and after

topics.title: Law of Constant Proportions
objectives: Student can state the law of constant proportions and Proust’s role in it
Student can calculate the mass ratio of elements in a compound such as water
visualIdeas: water from a river and a lab shown with the same 1:8 hydrogen to oxygen mass ratio

topics.title: Dalton’s Atomic Theory
objectives: Student can list the postulates of Dalton’s atomic theory
Student can explain how the theory accounts for the laws of chemical combination
visualIdeas: a list of Dalton’s postulates with a small picture beside each

topics.title: How Atoms Combine: Covalent Bonds
objectives: Student can explain that atoms share electrons to form covalent bonds and molecules
Student can draw electron dot structures for molecules with single, double and triple bonds
visualIdeas: electron dot diagrams for H₂, O₂ and N₂ showing single, double and triple bonds

topics.title: How Atoms Combine: Ionic Bonds
objectives: Student can explain how the transfer of electrons forms cations and anions
Student can describe the formation of an ionic compound such as sodium chloride
visualIdeas: sodium giving an electron to chlorine to form Na⁺ and Cl⁻ held together

topics.title: Writing Chemical Formulae
objectives: Student can write chemical formulae of covalent compounds from valencies
Student can write chemical formulae of ionic compounds, including those with polyatomic ions, using the criss-cross method
visualIdeas: a criss-cross diagram for aluminium oxide with valencies swapped into subscripts

topics.title: Properties of Ionic and Covalent Compounds
objectives: Student can compare ionic and covalent compounds by melting point, solubility and electrical conductivity
Student can explain why salt solution conducts electricity while sugar solution does not
visualIdeas: a bulb glowing in salt solution and staying dark in sugar solution

topics.title: Molecular Mass and Formula Unit Mass
objectives: Student can calculate the molecular mass of a covalent compound from atomic masses in u
Student can calculate the formula unit mass of an ionic compound
visualIdeas: a worked calculation of the mass of H₂O and of NaCl using atomic masses

topics.title: Production of Sound
objectives: Student can explain that sound is produced by vibrating objects
Student can use a tuning fork to show the vibrations that produce sound
visualIdeas: a tuning fork touching water and making splashes

topics.title: Propagation of Sound
objectives: Student can explain that sound needs a material medium to travel
Student can describe the bell jar experiment showing that sound cannot travel through a vacuum
visualIdeas: a ringing bell inside a jar as the air is pumped out and the sound fades

topics.title: Sound Waves
objectives: Student can describe sound as a mechanical, longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions
Student can distinguish longitudinal waves from transverse waves
visualIdeas: a slinky showing compressions and rarefactions beside a rope showing a transverse wave

topics.title: Energy of Sound Waves
objectives: Student can explain that sound waves carry energy from the source through the medium
Student can explain, using grains on a stretched sheet that jump when a loud sound is made nearby, that energy is transferred while the particles of the medium are not carried along
visualIdeas: grains on a rubber sheet stretched over a bowl, jumping when a metal plate is struck nearby

topics.title: Graphical Representation of a Sound Wave
objectives: Student can plot how the density of the medium varies with distance at an instant, with crests above and troughs below the average density
Student can relate compressions and rarefactions to the crests and troughs of the graph
visualIdeas: a row of air particles above a wave graph, with compressions lined up with peaks

topics.title: Wavelength, Frequency, Time Period and Amplitude
objectives: Student can define wavelength, frequency (in hertz), time period and amplitude of a sound wave
Student can relate the amplitude of a wave to the intensity of sound
visualIdeas: a labelled wave with wavelength and amplitude marked and a clock for the time period

topics.title: Speed of Sound
objectives: Student can use the relation speed = frequency × wavelength
Student can explain how the speed of sound depends on the medium and on temperature
visualIdeas: a table of the speed of sound in air, water and steel

topics.title: Human Perception of Sound
objectives: Student can relate loudness to amplitude and pitch to frequency
Student can state the audible range of humans as about 20 Hz to 20 kHz and the decibel as a unit of loudness
Student can explain how quality (timbre) lets us tell two sounds of the same pitch apart
visualIdeas: two waves with the same frequency but different amplitudes, and two with different frequencies

topics.title: Reflection of Sound: Echo and Reverberation
objectives: Student can explain how an echo is formed and the minimum distance needed to hear one
Student can explain reverberation and how halls are designed to reduce it
visualIdeas: a person shouting at a cliff with the sound returning
an auditorium with sound-absorbing panels

topics.title: Ultrasonic and Infrasonic Waves, and their Applications
objectives: Student can distinguish ultrasound and infrasound from audible sound by frequency
Student can describe echolocation by bats and dolphins and the working of SONAR
visualIdeas: a ship sending SONAR pulses to the sea bed and timing the echo
a bat locating an insect by echoes

topics.title: Asexual Reproduction and Vegetative Propagation
objectives: Student can define asexual reproduction as producing offspring from a single parent
Student can describe vegetative propagation by cutting, layering, grafting and tissue culture
Student can explain why vegetative propagation is helpful in agriculture
visualIdeas: a rose cutting rooting in soil, a layered branch and a graft joint side by side

topics.title: Budding and Spore Formation
objectives: Student can describe budding in yeast and hydra
Student can describe spore formation in bread mould and the conditions spores need to grow
visualIdeas: a hydra with a bud, and bread mould with hyphae and spore sacs

topics.title: Sexual Reproduction and Meiosis
objectives: Student can explain that sexual reproduction involves the fusion of male and female gametes to form a zygote
Student can explain how meiosis creates variations in sexual reproduction
visualIdeas: two gametes fusing into a zygote with the halved chromosome number shown

topics.title: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
objectives: Student can label the stamen (anther, filament) and pistil (stigma, style, ovary, ovule) of a flower
Student can describe the flower as the reproductive organ of flowering plants
visualIdeas: a labelled cut-away flower showing stamens and pistil

topics.title: Pollination and Pollination Strategies
objectives: Student can distinguish self-pollination from cross-pollination
Student can describe how agents and flower features help pollination and reproductive success
visualIdeas: a bee carrying pollen from one flower to another

topics.title: Fertilisation and Seed Formation
objectives: Student can describe how a pollen tube carries the male gamete to the ovule for fertilisation
Student can explain how the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit
visualIdeas: a pollen tube growing down the style to the ovule
an ovary developing into a fruit with seeds

topics.title: Sexual Reproduction and its Variations in Animals

topics.title: Kingdom Plantae
